title: Pauri 26, sound: amul gun

segments.voice: Yesterday, daat, the gift, even in hard things. Your line was even this is a gift. Today, Japji walks into a marketplace.

An old bazaar in Punjab. Spice sellers calling out. Cloth merchants unrolling silk. A man with brass scales weighing lentils, a woman haggling over the price of mangoes. Everything has a price, and everybody's arguing about it. Guru Nanak knew this world well; tradition says he worked for a time as a storekeeper, weighing out grain. So Pauri 26 borrows the language of the market: traders, trade, storehouses, scales. And then it breaks every price tag.
screen: `AN OLD PUNJAB BAZAAR.` → `EVERYTHING HAS A PRICE.` → `PAURI 26 BREAKS THE TAGS.`

segments.voice: The first line, in the original: amul gun amul vaapaar. Four words. Amul, a-MOOL: without price, priceless. It's built like asankh, countless: a, not, plus mul, price. More on amul tomorrow. Gun, said with the u of put, not like the English word: virtues, qualities, the good things in a person, or in God. Vaapaar, vaa-PAAR: trade, business, dealing, the same word Punjabis still use for running a shop. So: priceless the virtues, priceless the trade. The stanza keeps going, in paraphrase: priceless the traders, priceless the storehouses, priceless those who come to deal, priceless what they take away, priceless the scales, priceless the weights. Every piece of the market, one after another, stamped amul. Hear the drumbeat: the same word striking at the start of each half, the way asankh did three weeks ago. Say it quickly and it sounds like a merchant calling out his wares; slowly, like a prayer. Borrowing the market isn't despising it. Sikhs are known for honest work, kirat karni, and many are shopkeepers and traders. The point is that for the virtues of the One, and the dealing between the soul and God, the scale has no numbers on it.
screen: `AMUL — WITHOUT PRICE.` · `GUN — VIRTUES, QUALITIES.` · `VAAPAAR — TRADE, DEALING.` · `EVERY PART OF THE MARKET.` · then, large: `AMUL GUN.`

segments.voice: Say the line aloud, amul gun, amul vaapaar: once brisk and clear like a merchant calling out, once slowly like a prayer, once as a whisper. Then let one good quality in someone you love come to mind: their patience, their humor, their kindness. Don't put a price on it; just hold it.
Vaapaar, trade, dealing. It opens amul gun, amul vaapaar: priceless the virtues, priceless the trade, and every part of the market after them.
Your line: amul gun. Some of the best things carry no price tag at all. Day two hundred five, done.

howItsDone: Pauri 26 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs, for whom honest work, kirat karni, is one of the three pillars of daily life, hear its market words with special closeness.
